# TypeScript sketches for TouchDesigner This is the complete TouchDesigner-facing script guide for this generated project, including instructions for coding agents. It is usable offline and is created alongside `tsconfig.json` and `sketches/` by **Create Template Project**. The SDK declarations are the exact API contracts; this guide explains how to use them. It does not attempt to document the full p5 drawing API. Start with the setup and example catalog below, then use these reference sections: - [Agent workflow and runtime boundaries](#agent-workflow-and-runtime-boundaries) - [CHOP API](#chop-api) - [TOP API](#top-api) - [WebGPU lifecycle in this host](#webgpu-lifecycle-in-this-host) - [Declared parameter reference](#declared-parameter-reference) - [Pulses and callback ordering](#pulses-and-callback-ordering) - [TimeContext and independent tasks](#timecontext-and-independent-tasks) - [Execution modes and latency](#execution-modes-and-latency) - [Native MIDI API](#native-midi-api) - [File API](#file-api) - [UDP and OSC API](#udp-and-osc-api) - [Build, activation and cleanup](#build-activation-and-cleanup) - [Logging, diagnostics and verification](#logging-diagnostics-and-verification) ## Quick start Open this folder in VS Code. The local SDK and tsconfig provide TypeScript types without installing Node or an editor extension. In an avTools TOP's **Build** page, select `sketches/background/main.ts` as **TypeScript File**. In an avTools CHOP, select `sketches/channels/main.ts` and set **Output Channels** to `value ticks`, **Output Samples** to `1`. A wired input channel named `value` is doubled; `ticks` advances independently with TimeContext. The default TOP exposes Size, Color and Speed on its **Controls** page. The default CHOP exposes Gain, Offset and Tick Interval; its initial value behavior is still twice the input. Adjust these controls without editing code. The Create Template Project button configures the operator that created this folder. For a TOP it sets **Sketch → Width = 1280, Height = 720** (720p). Change those parameters for another resolution; use `frame.width`/`frame.height` in the sketch. Add more .ts entries anywhere under this tsconfig and select them on other operators. Share helpers using ordinary imports. No manifest or bundle paths are needed. Each operator checks its entry and dependencies; unrelated sketches can have errors without blocking it. All operators use their own runtime state. Automatic Builds reloads changed bundles after saving. Build Script requests a manual build. Type errors preserve that entry's last working bundle. Runtime caches live in `.avtools/entries/`; these are disposable and not source files. Import TimeContext functions normally from `@avtools/core-timing`. Automatic Builds compiles; Automatic Reload controls activation. Reload adopts the latest successful bundle; Reset restarts the active bundle. Each activation starts fresh module/global state. Installed npm packages and linked/shared source work, but dependencies must use APIs supported by embedded V8/TD. Node and browser APIs are not supplied. Package installation is separate from the native builder. This mixed starter includes TOP GPU types; use `sdk/packages/native-webgpu/td-runtime.d.ts` instead of `td-top-runtime.d.ts` in `tsconfig.json` for a CHOP-only environment. Local WGSL files can be imported as strings. Shader conventions `.material.wgsl`, `.strokeMaterial.wgsl`, `.fragFunc.wgsl` and `.compute.wgsl` generate typed wrappers under `generated/`, retaining the shader's project-relative directories. Only wrappers used by the selected entry affect its build. Optional CLI: `avtools-build build-file sketches/background/main.ts top` or `avtools-build watch-file sketches/channels/main.ts chop`. No terminal watcher is required when using the plugin's Automatic Builds toggle. ## Script-declared controls Try `sketches/parameters/picture.ts` on a TOP or `sketches/parameters/channels.ts` on a CHOP (Output Channels: `value`). Their exported `parameters` object creates native controls on a **Controls** page, including named pulse buttons. Read `host.params` in setup/timing/CHOP callbacks or `frame.params` in TOP draw/pulses. Use `ChopHost` / `Draw` for typed values. Declarations must be literal data exported directly by the entry file; helper functions, imported declarations and spreads are not supported. Normal sketch code/imports remain unrestricted by this rule. Names start with an uppercase letter followed by lowercase letters/digits. Compatible names and types retain TD values, expressions, exports and bindings across schema edits. Add/remove or change defaults/ranges to update controls. Use a new name to change a type. A schema edit recreates the native instance and restarts the sketch, so it can cause a brief interruption. Ordinary code edits use the normal JS reload path. Automatic Reload off retains the active code **and** controls; Reload adopts both, while Reset restarts the active version. Compile/schema errors preserve last-working code/controls. Runtime errors after activation require fixing the script or Reset; they do not roll back a successfully installed schema. ## Example catalog Select one entry per operator using **Build → TypeScript File**. All examples share this project's SDK; you do not need to generate another template per OP. | Entry under `sketches/` | Operator and configuration | Demonstrates | | --- | --- | --- | | `background/main.ts` | TOP | p5 draw callback and shared helper import | | `channels/main.ts` | CHOP, outputs `value ticks`, 1 sample | Current inputs, same-cook math, independent timing | | `parameters/picture.ts` | TOP | Color, menu, toggle, size, Shuffle pulse | | `parameters/channels.ts` | CHOP, output `value`, 1 sample | Animate pulse, replaceable TimeContext ramp, latest parameter/input reads | | `parameters/all-controls.ts` | CHOP, outputs `value count x y z red alpha textlength pulses`, 1 sample | Every control type, custom page, typed snapshots and named pulses | | `buffers/interpolate.ts` | CHOP, outputs `x y`, 10000 samples | Blend two XY input buffers, missing samples, reusable output arrays | | `inputs/picture.ts` | TOP, optional wired TOP and Controls CHOP | Image input, named CHOP reads, missing-input fallback | | `timing/picture.ts` | TOP | Independent TimeContext loop updates state; draw presents it, cleanup on reload | | `osc/channels.ts` | CHOP, outputs `value target messages port`, 1 sample | Async JSON file read, incoming OSC, TimeContext easing, OSC reply | | `osc/picture.ts` | TOP | Async JSON file read, OSC position control | | `osc/udp.ts` | CHOP, outputs `port bytes messages`, 1 sample | Raw UDP reception and echo | For the buffer example, wire two CHOPs with `x` and `y` channels and matching sample counts. Enable **Wait for Current Result** when same-cook data is required. The Blend slider interpolates each point. For the input TOP example, a CHOP channel named `size` controls the circle; an optional TOP supplies its background. ## API notes - TOP `setup(p, host)` initializes state/resources; `draw(p, frame)` presents it. Use `frame.top(index)` for image inputs and `frame.chop(name)` for Controls CHOP samples. `host.chop(name)` reads the latest accepted snapshot from a timer. - CHOP `setup(host)` initializes persistent outputs; synchronous `onCook(host, frame)` transforms current inputs. `inputs.get(name, input, sample)` reads one sample; `inputs.samples(name, input)` returns an owned Float32Array copy. `outputs.set` changes one sample; `outputs.setSamples` copies a whole channel whose length must match Output Samples. Outputs retain their last values. - `onPulse` receives the exact declared parameter name (or Send Pulse event name). Read current input/parameter state in the handler. Pulses carry no arguments. - `host.params` exposes a fresh accepted snapshot; a local reference keeps its old values across `await`. Buffered modes retain their existing input/output latency. Parameter sampling adds no extra frame delay. - `host.onDispose` registers short synchronous cleanup. Reload/reset tears down the old runtime and timing tasks. Local state is recreated on each activation. ## Git and SDK restoration The plugin creates this `avtools-project/` directory inside the selected **Template Parent Folder**. Open this directory itself in VS Code. The button refuses to merge with an existing directory; other operators should select its existing entry files instead of pressing Create Template Project again. The included `.gitignore` excludes `/sdk/`, `/node_modules/`, build caches, generated shader wrappers and TD backups. Commit your sketches, tsconfig and README. Record the plugin distribution version used by your project. On another computer, create a temporary template with that same plugin version, copy its `sdk/` here, then open this folder in VS Code. Avoid overwriting deliberately modified SDK files. You can choose to vendor the SDK instead by removing the `/sdk/` ignore rule and committing it. ## Files and OSC / UDP Both hosts include `files`, `udp` and `osc`; no npm dependency is necessary. Select `sketches/osc/channels.ts` on a CHOP with Output Channels `value target messages port` for TimeContext easing driven by `/target` OSC messages. Select `sketches/osc/picture.ts` on a TOP for `/x` position control. `sketches/osc/udp.ts` is a raw UDP echo example (channels `port bytes messages`). These entries load `config.json` asynchronously during setup. Relative file paths resolve beside the entrypoint. Use `await host.files.readText(path)` or `readBytes(path)`; missing/unreadable files reject. Regular files up to 64 MiB are supported, with four simultaneous reads. Reset rereads assets. `const osc = await host.osc.open({port: 9000})` listens on localhost. Use an available port for each instance, or `port: 0` to select one automatically; `osc.localAddress` tells you the chosen port. LAN reception requires an explicit `address: '0.0.0.0'`. Numeric IPv4/IPv6 and `localhost` are supported. `osc.onMessage((message, remote) => ...)` receives typed `message.args` and an OSC address. Send with `osc.send({address: '/reply', args: [0.5]}, remote)`. Plain numbers send float32; `{type: 'i', value: 42}` sends int32. Catch send promise rejections and use `osc.onError()` for malformed incoming packets. Bundles deliver immediately and expose their raw bigint timetag to the handler. Callbacks run independently of TD cooking, on the same JS worker as timing callbacks. They can read current host state and update state/output immediately. A TD cook presents the latest output. Reload/Reset closes sockets automatically; changing a setup Port parameter needs Reset. Raw `host.udp.open()` has the same lifecycle, but receives/sends Uint8Array datagrams. Monitor `host.udp.droppedDatagrams` for overflow of the 256 packet / 4 MiB receive queue. See the SDK's `td-io.d.ts` for method/type descriptions and limits. ## Agent workflow and runtime boundaries 1. Open this project root, containing `tsconfig.json`, in your IDE. Preserve the SDK and its TypeScript environment; do not add `DOM` or Node ambient types to silence errors for APIs that do not exist in the plugin. 2. Decide whether the entry produces channels (CHOP) or an image (TOP). Import the matching callback/host types with `import type`. These are declarations, not runtime modules to instantiate. 3. Write an entry under `sketches/`; helpers may use normal relative imports, TypeScript aliases, linked source and installed npm packages. Select that entry in the operator's **Build → TypeScript File**. No manifest is needed. 4. For a CHOP, tell the user the exact **Output Channels** and **Output Samples** needed. JavaScript cannot add output channels dynamically. For a TOP, choose Width/Height on its Sketch page; the initialized default is 1280×720. 5. Save and check the operator's build diagnostics. A successful typecheck is not a runtime test: verify actual outputs, pulses and reload behavior in TD. Each instance has its own V8 isolate and dedicated JavaScript worker. Module variables are persistent within that activation, independent of other instances, including instances using the same entry file. There is no shared JS global state between operators. Connect CHOP/TOP inputs or use explicit communication such as OSC to exchange data. The worker does **not** expose TD's Python API: there is no `op()`, `parent()`, `me`, parameter setter, arbitrary DAT access or network-creation API in a sketch. Use the host inputs, declared controls, pulse handlers and outputs described here. Python snippets in the pre-trigger section belong in an Execute DAT, not a `.ts` entry. The native builder bundles modules before execution; it is not a Node runtime or a general runtime module loader. Supported global host facilities, in addition to standard ECMAScript objects: | Facility | Contract | | --- | --- | | `console.log/info/warn/error/debug` | Per-operator bounded logs; see diagnostics below | | `performance.now()` | Monotonic milliseconds relative to runtime creation | | `setTimeout(fn, ms, ...args)`, `clearTimeout(id)` | Independent wall-clock timers; numeric handles | | `setImmediate(fn, ...args)`, `clearImmediate(id)` | Deferred worker tasks; no promised ordering relative to timeouts | | `queueMicrotask(fn)` | Microtask after the current synchronous work | | `requestAnimationFrame(fn)`, `cancelAnimationFrame(id)` | One-shot callback on an accepted TD request, not a display clock | | `Event`, `EventTarget` | Basic listeners, `once`, dispatch and cancellation; no DOM tree | | `AbortController`, `AbortSignal` | Abort reason, listeners and `throwIfAborted`; no static signal helpers | | `DOMException`, global event listeners | Includes cancelable `unhandledrejection` events | | `crypto.randomUUID()` | OS-backed UUID generation | | TOP WebGPU globals | Dawn types/constants; use the supplied `host.device` | There is no `window`, `document`, browser canvas, `navigator.gpu`, `fetch`, `WebSocket`, `process`, Node `fs`/`dgram`, Node `Buffer`, `setInterval`, or global `TextEncoder`/`TextDecoder` API. Use `host.files`, `host.udp`, and `host.osc` for the supported I/O. npm packages are usable when their executed code fits this host; installing packages requires your own package manager. A successful bundle does not make unavailable platform APIs work. CHOPs have no GPU device, even though this mixed project's editor profile includes TOP types. Timeout delays below 1 ms, above 2,147,483,647 ms, or NaN become 1 ms; fractional milliseconds truncate. Timers are independent of TD cooks but share the instance's JS thread, so synchronous work can delay them. They are not hard realtime. Exact declarations are in `sdk/packages/native-webgpu/`: `td-chop.d.ts`, `td-sketch.d.ts`, `td-parameters.d.ts`, `td-io.d.ts`, `td-runtime.d.ts`, `td-top-runtime.d.ts`, and `td-types/p5.d.ts`. Do not make `onCook`/`onPulse` async. Launch background tasks from them when necessary and return immediately. A task may change persistent state/outputs later; it cannot extend the current synchronous cook across an `await`. ### Input channels Up to four wired CHOP inputs are addressed by zero-based connector index. | Method | Behavior | | --- | --- | | `host.inputs.get(name, input = 0, sample?)` | One number; omitted sample means the **last sample** of the channel | | `host.inputs.samples(name, input = 0)` | Owned `Float32Array` copy of the whole channel | | `host.inputs.names(input = 0)` | Array of channel names | Missing channels/inputs/sample indexes read as `0`; missing whole channels return an empty array. Changing a returned array does not modify TD or the host snapshot. Each synchronous callback sees a stable accepted snapshot. After `await`, a fresh read may observe a later accepted request. No worker-side read pulls a new TD cook: inputs remain at the last accepted values while upstream cooking is stopped. ### Output channels Configure **Script → Output Channels** as space-separated unique identifiers, for example `value velocity`, and **Output Samples**, normally `1`. Channel names start with a letter or underscore and contain letters, digits or underscores. Limits are 128 characters per name, 1024 channels, and 1,048,576 total samples (channel count × sample count). Output sample rate follows TD's frame rate and start index is zero; this is a fixed-size output buffer, not CHOP time slicing. | Member | Behavior | | --- | --- | | `host.outputs.sampleCount` | Configured samples per channel for this activation | | `host.outputs.set(name, value, sample = 0)` | Write one sample of a configured channel | | `host.outputs.get(name, sample = 0)` | Read persistent worker state immediately; missing data gives `0` | | `host.outputs.setSamples(name, values)` | Copy exactly `sampleCount` finite numbers from an array-like object | | `host.outputs.samples(name)` | Owned copy of persistent output state; missing channel gives an empty array | | `host.outputs.names()` | Configured output channel names | Writes to unknown channels, invalid indexes, wrong buffer lengths, or values that are not finite float32 numbers throw. Outputs start at zero and retain their last values until changed. Changing an array returned by `samples()` does not write output; call `setSamples()`. Input/output copies have real CPU cost: read each whole input once per callback, reuse your working arrays, and publish once per channel instead of copying in an inner loop. The host publishes complete callback-turn snapshots. TD never sees a half-written array from a synchronous callback. Different continuations of an async function can publish separately. Independent timers/OSC callbacks can update outputs without `onCook`; TD presents the latest publication when it next cooks. A complete same-cook transform (Output Channels `value`, Output Samples `1`): ```ts // Target: chop import type { ChopHost } from '@avtools/native-webgpu/td-chop'; import type { ParameterDefinitions } from '@avtools/native-webgpu/td-parameters'; export const parameters = { Gain: { type: 'float', default: 2, min: 0, max: 4 }, Clear: { type: 'pulse' }, } as const satisfies ParameterDefinitions; type Host = ChopHost; let held = 0; export function onCook(host: Host) { held = host.inputs.get('value') * host.params.Gain; host.outputs.set('value', held); } export function onPulse(name: string, host: Host) { if (name === 'Clear') { held = 0; host.outputs.set('value', held); } // onCook follows this pulse and may overwrite the value in this same request. } ``` `ChopFrame` fields: `frame` (TD timeline frame), `absFrame` (TD absolute frame), `rate` (frames/second), `time` (`(frame - 1) / rate`, seconds), and `deltaSeconds`. In buffered mode `deltaSeconds` accumulates elapsed absolute TD time across coalesced requests; backwards absolute time resets its anchor. Timeline seeks and loops do not rewind the independent TimeContext clock. See `sketches/buffers/interpolate.ts` for interpolation between two 10,000-point XY buffers. Bundled fonts initialize the renderer automatically; this guide leaves p5 drawing/font methods to the SDK's p5 declarations. ### WebGPU lifecycle in this host You can use raw WebGPU, `@avtools/power2d/raw` and `@avtools/shader-fx/raw` for your rendering or compute work. The TD integration differences from a browser are: - **Device:** use `host.device` in TOP setup. The host already selected Dawn's Metal adapter and created the device. There is no `navigator.gpu`, adapter negotiation or browser canvas to configure. Check the supplied device's `features`/`limits` if your code needs an optional capability; an adapter's possible feature is not necessarily enabled on this device. - **Output:** render into your own same-device texture, then pass it to `p.image({texture}, 0, 0, frame.width, frame.height)` in draw. This is the current presentation bridge even if you use no other p5 drawing functions. There is no exported `render(device)` callback, canvas swapchain, or return-a-texture output API. A `draw` export is still required. - **Texture contract:** use a sampleable 2D color texture (the simple path is single-sample `rgba8unorm` with `TEXTURE_BINDING`, plus the usage your renderer needs). Resolve multisampling and visualize depth/integer/storage data into such a color texture first. Presentation expects straight alpha and top-left UVs; `p.image({texture, flipY: true}, ...)` handles an opposite image origin. - **Submission:** submit your own passes on `host.device.queue` before calling `p.image`. Queue ordering handles their dependency on the host's later image submission. Do not wait for `queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()` or map a readback just to present an image. Keep the texture alive and unchanged through the end of draw; `p.image` queues its use, it does not take an immediate pixel copy. - **Frames:** TD invokes synchronous draw on accepted cook requests. RAF is a TD request event, not a screen refresh loop. Timers may update CPU state independently; render/present it in draw. The host begins/ends the renderer frame and handles output readback/TD upload or Syphon after draw returns. - **Lifetime:** allocate long-lived resources in setup using `p.width`/`p.height`. Reload, Reset, resize and operator deletion retire this activation and its device. Setup runs again with a new device after restart; no pipeline, texture or buffer from the old device is reusable. Do not destroy `host.device` yourself. Use `host.onDispose` for your library's synchronous cleanup; host tracking also destroys buffers/textures created through the guarded device. - **Inputs and isolation:** `frame.top(i)` is an owned-by-host uploaded input, not a borrowed TD-native GPU texture. Do not destroy it. Each TOP has its own device/isolate, so GPU objects cannot be shared across TOP instances. GPU validation/device-loss errors surface through operator diagnostics; Reset creates a fresh runtime rather than browser-style canvas recovery. Minimal lifecycle example: the raw pass creates the image; p5 is used only to present its texture. Save as a TOP entry. It needs no external shader or input. ```ts // Target: top // Example: raw-webgpu-lifecycle import type { Setup, Draw } from '@avtools/native-webgpu/td-sketch'; let device: GPUDevice; let image: GPUTexture; export const setup: Setup = (p, host) => { device = host.device; image = device.createTexture({ size: [p.width, p.height], format: 'rgba8unorm', usage: GPUTextureUsage.RENDER_ATTACHMENT | GPUTextureUsage.TEXTURE_BINDING, }); host.onDispose(() => image.destroy()); // Library renderers can register renderer.dispose() here instead. }; export const draw: Draw = (p, frame) => { const encoder = device.createCommandEncoder(); const pass = encoder.beginRenderPass({ colorAttachments: [{ view: image.createView(), clearValue: { r: 0.1, g: 0.3, b: 0.8, a: 1 }, loadOp: 'clear', storeOp: 'store', }], }); // Your normal WebGPU render/compute workflow produces the image here. pass.end(); device.queue.submit([encoder.finish()]); p.image({ texture: image }, 0, 0, frame.width, frame.height); }; ``` Power2D/ShaderFX follow this same pattern: initialize with `host.device`, render in draw, present the library's output texture with `p.image`, and dispose the library's resources on teardown. Prefer their `/raw` entrypoints over browser- or Babylon-specific hosts. WGSL imports and generated wrappers work through the native builder described below; no browser canvas setup is involved. ## Declared parameter reference Use `export const parameters = { ... } as const satisfies ParameterDefinitions` directly in the TypeScript entrypoint. Every definition has `type` and optional `label` and `page`. Default page is **Controls**. `as const` preserves literal menu options and tuple types for `ChopHost` / `Draw`. | `type` | JavaScript value | Default and additional fields | | --- | --- | --- | | `float`, `int` | `number` | Default `0`; optional `min`, `max`, `clamp` | | `toggle` | `boolean` | Default `false` | | `string` | `string` | Default `''` | | `menu` | Union of option strings | Required `options`; optional matching `labels`; default first option | | `xy` | Readonly pair | Default zeros; optional `min`, `max`, `clamp` | | `xyz`, `rgb` | Readonly triple | Default zeros; optional `min`, `max`, `clamp` | | `rgba` | Readonly quadruple | Default zeros; optional `min`, `max`, `clamp` | | `pulse` | No value; event only | Delivered by exact name to `onPulse` | `default` sets a new control's initial value. RGB/RGBA values come from TD's working color space. Nonfinite numeric expressions sample as zero. Names must be an uppercase letter followed by lowercase letters/digits: `Speed`, `Bpm`, `Offset2` are valid; `mySpeed` and `MySpeed` are not. Avoid built-in control names and tuple-component collisions. Use your own page names rather than built-in Build, Sketch, Script, Output, Diagnostics or Legacy Build pages. Maximum: 64 declarations and 32 KiB metadata per entry. Metadata must be literal data in that export. No imported schema, re-export, spread, computed key, function, variable reference or generated default expression is supported. This restriction applies only to UI metadata, not ordinary code. Raw JavaScript/DAT scripts do not get builder-extracted parameter declarations. Reads are immutable snapshots, sampled with other accepted inputs without an extra frame of latency. Read `host.params` again after an `await` to observe new accepted values; `const saved = host.params` intentionally keeps the old snapshot. Undeclared properties are `undefined` at runtime and rejected by generic types. You cannot set TD controls by assigning to `host.params`. Compatible names/types retain TD values, expressions, exports and bindings. Changing a default does not overwrite a user's current value. Added controls get defaults; removed controls disappear. Changing type under the same name is rejected: use a new name and reconnect bindings as necessary. A schema edit recreates the native instance, so expect a brief restart. An ordinary code edit restarts only the JavaScript runtime. Saved `.toe`/`.tox` files retain the declared control schema/values, not live JS variables or timing tasks. ## Pulses and callback ordering For an ad hoc event, set **Event Name** and press **Send Pulse** on Sketch (TOP) or Script (CHOP). For a dedicated button, declare a `pulse` parameter. Both call `onPulse` with the captured name. There is no event payload; read input channels and declared parameters in the handler. Missing input channels return zero as specified above; pulse parameters are absent from `host.params`. Accepted requests install inputs/parameters, complete setup if needed, resume existing frame waiters, dispatch queued pulse names FIFO, and then invoke `draw`/`onCook`. Thus onCook can overwrite a pulse's output in the same request. A pulse is not an independent realtime callback: it waits for an accepted TD request, even while wall-clock timers/OSC are running. Queue capacity is 256; overflow is reported. Buffered CHOP input replacement does not discard separately queued pulse names. The handler sees the snapshot accepted for delivery, not a historical snapshot captured at the button press. ## TimeContext and independent tasks Use ordinary imports from `@avtools/core-timing`. `launch` supplies a realtime context with `waitSec(seconds)` and tempo-aware `wait(beats)`; options include `bpm`, `rate`, `seed`, `debugName` and timer overrides. Its cancelable handle has `cancel()` and promise-like completion/error methods. `launchBrowser` additionally supplies `waitFrame()`: despite the name, it works with TD's provided RAF adapter. Other portable timing APIs remain available from the bundled source. A persistent CHOP animation (Output Channels `value`, Output Samples `1`): ```ts // Target: chop import { launch } from '@avtools/core-timing'; import type { ChopHost } from '@avtools/native-webgpu/td-chop'; export function setup(host: ChopHost) { const task = launch(async (ctx) => { while (true) { const target = host.inputs.get('target'); const current = host.outputs.get('value'); host.outputs.set('value', current + (target - current) * 0.1); await ctx.waitSec(1 / 120); } }); // Error policy here is explicit: report a failed task and leave its last value. task.catch((error) => console.error('Animation stopped:', error)); host.onDispose(() => task.cancel()); // Return now. Awaiting this endless task would prevent setup from completing. } ``` Keep animation state in ordinary variables or persistent CHOP outputs. An independent loop reads the latest accepted host state, updates its own state, and lets TD's cook/render path present it. No extra "next frame" object is needed. For elapsed real time, measure `performance.now()` or use the timing library; do not assume each callback arrives exactly at its requested interval. `waitSec` and `setTimeout` continue without TD cooks, including paused playback. `waitFrame`/RAF advance only on **accepted requests**, after input capture and before pulses/draw/onCook. A busy TOP or coalesced CHOP does not replay skipped requests. Repeated cooks in the same TD frame can deliver multiple frame events. Frame waits neither pull TD input data nor synchronize to a display refresh. While paused, host inputs/parameters remain at their last accepted values. Launch independent tasks from setup or pulses, not once per draw/cook unless that is deliberate. Cancel or supersede an older animation when retriggering; otherwise several tasks may write the same state. For full reload, the isolate boundary stops all old tasks even if application cancellation cleanup cannot run. ## Execution modes and latency | Operator | Default | Wait for Current Result on | Toggle off | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CHOP | On | TD waits for the accepted current inputs and onCook result | Offers inputs and collects latest complete publication | | TOP | Off | TD waits for earlier work and renders current inputs | Submits when idle and collects a finished image | Blocking CHOPs have no intentional extra frame delay for simple input/output math; they do consume TD's frame budget. A chain of buffered CHOPs can accumulate latency because each reads the latest completed upstream output. Use blocking mode where a same-cook dependency matters. Changing this toggle preserves state. Buffered output is not guaranteed to be exactly one frame late. Completion may be ready in the same cook or later; busy workers and long tasks can increase age. A CHOP coalesces pending inputs, so intermediate snapshots may be skipped. A TOP skips new input captures while busy. Independent instances can work concurrently, but they still share CPU/GPU/memory bandwidth and TD must collect their output. TOP CPU output uses RGBA8 readback from Dawn and a TD upload. Wired image inputs also require TD download and Dawn upload; they are not zero-copy textures shared with the script. Buffering moves waits off the ordinary TD cook path, not all transfer or submission costs. Named CHOP controls use CPU snapshots instead. ### Optional TOP pre-trigger mode Enable **Output → Pre-trigger Mode** on participating TOPs and use one Execute DAT with Frame Start enabled. Early submission gives workers time before later collection. **Wait for Current Result** is ignored in this mode. Ordinary cooks only collect; without a coordinator the TOP cannot submit new renders. This minimal coordinator belongs in an Execute DAT in the enclosing component: ```python # TouchDesigner Execute DAT: enable Frame Start. def onFrameStart(frame): nodes = sorted( (n for n in parent().findChildren(type=TOP, parName='Pretrigger') if n.valid and not n.bypass and hasattr(n.par, 'Pretriggerpulse') and n.par.Pretrigger.eval()), key=lambda n: n.path, ) try: for n in nodes: n.par.Pretriggerpulse.pulse() n.cook(force=True) # Optional: cook independent work here, before collecting these TOPs. # Do not sleep or poll; avoid branches depending on these same TOPs. finally: for n in nodes: if n.valid and not n.bypass: n.cook(force=True) return ``` A ready current-frame image is collected; otherwise the previous image remains. There is no guarantee of same-frame completion. Inputs are captured on submission, so anything updated afterwards belongs to a later accepted request. Input image transfers still have TD/GPU synchronization costs. Forced collection is necessary because TD can cache a prior cook within the same frame. ### Optional Syphon output On Output, enable **Enable Syphon** and choose **Syphon Name** for the instance. A Syphon receiver can consume that image. With **Syphon Only (1px TOP)** enabled, the plugin skips normal full-size CPU output readback and publishes through Syphon; the wired TOP becomes a 1×1 placeholder. Use a Syphon receiver in TD for the full image. Enabling Syphon without Syphon Only keeps normal CPU TOP output as well. Wired image inputs still use CPU transfer. Use unique names for instances. ## File API Both hosts provide: | Member | Result | | --- | --- | | `host.files.baseDirectory` | Base path for this active script | | `await host.files.readText(path)` | UTF-8 string; invalid encoding rejects | | `await host.files.readBytes(path)` | Owned `Uint8Array` | Relative paths resolve beside the selected TypeScript/source entry, not beside its emitted `.avtools` bundle or necessarily the `.toe`. DAT scripts use TD's `project.folder`; legacy manifest entries use their Project Directory. Absolute paths, `../` and symlinks are supported with TD's macOS permissions. Only regular files up to 64 MiB are accepted, with at most four pending reads per instance. Missing files, permission errors, directories and oversized files reject. Use `async setup` for initialization and validate parsed JSON before use. Asset file changes alone do not rebuild TypeScript; Reset rereads setup assets, or your code can explicitly reread them. There are no file-write/directory APIs. See `sketches/osc/config.json` and the matching TOP/CHOP entries for complete examples. ```ts // Target: chop import type { ChopHost } from '@avtools/native-webgpu/td-chop'; export async function setup(host: ChopHost) { // Create config.json beside this entry, for example: {"initialValue": 0.25}. const config: unknown = JSON.parse(await host.files.readText('./config.json')); if (typeof config !== 'object' || config === null || !('initialValue' in config) || typeof config.initialValue !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(config.initialValue)) { throw new Error('config.json needs a finite initialValue'); } host.outputs.set('value', config.initialValue); } ``` ## UDP and OSC API Import types from `@avtools/native-webgpu/td-io`. Both hosts expose `await host.udp.open(options?)` and `await host.osc.open(options?)`. Options are `{address?: string, port?: number}`; defaults are `127.0.0.1` and port `0` (choose an available port). A sender also uses an opened socket. | Socket member | UDP | OSC | | --- | --- | --- | | `localAddress` | `{address, port}` | Same | | `send(payload, remote)` | `Uint8Array` → `Promise` | `OscMessage` or `OscBundle` → `Promise` | | `onMessage(fn)` | `(bytes, remote) => void` | `(message, remote) => void` | | `onError(fn)` | `(error: Error) => void` | Includes malformed OSC errors | | `close()` | Idempotent | Idempotent | `remote` is `{address: string, port: number}`. Each listener registration returns an unsubscribe function. Numeric IPv4/IPv6 and `localhost` are supported; DNS, multicast and broadcast options are not. Bind `0.0.0.0` or `::` explicitly for LAN reception. A port is exclusive, so duplicate binds reject. For several instances, use different ports or let `0` choose one and inspect `localAddress.port`. Open/send errors reject their promises. Send resolves on OS acceptance, not remote receipt. UDP may lose or reorder datagrams. Native receive failure calls `onError` and closes the socket. Reload, Reset, failed-generation invalidation and destruction close sockets and suppress stale callbacks automatically. If a Port control is read only during setup, press Reset after changing it. Callbacks run on the same JS owner as timing, independently of TD cooking. They may update ordinary state or CHOP output; TD still needs a cook to show it. Keep callbacks short. Do not assume an async listener is awaited: explicitly handle promises it launches. Exceptions follow the sketch's normal error policy. Limits per instance: 16 sockets, 64 in-flight native sends, 128 pending native operations, 65,507 bytes per UDP datagram, and a receive queue of 256 packets / 4 MiB. `host.udp.droppedDatagrams` counts native queue overflow, not all network loss. Outgoing bytes are copied. Listeners on one UDP socket receive the same owned packet object; copy it before independent mutation. ### OSC payloads and typed arguments Send a message as `{address: '/gain', args: [0.5]}`. `args` is optional. Send a bundle as `{timetag: 1n, packets: [messageOrBundle, ...]}`. Incoming messages have `address`, typed `args`, and a raw bigint `timetag`. Incoming args are **objects**, not bare numbers: narrow `arg.type` before using `arg.value`. | Outgoing value | OSC tag | | --- | --- | | `number` | `f` (float32) | | `string` | `s` | | `boolean` | `T` / `F` | | `null` | `N` | | `bigint` | `h` (int64) | | `Uint8Array` | `b` (blob) | Explicit arguments support these shapes: - `{type: 'i' | 'f' | 'd' | 'c' | 'r', value: number}` - `{type: 'h' | 't', value: bigint}` - `{type: 's' | 'S', value: string}` - `{type: 'b' | 'm', value: Uint8Array}` (`m` is four-byte MIDI data) - `{type: 'T' | 'F' | 'N' | 'I'}` (no value field) - `{type: 'array', value: OscArgument[]}` (nested typed arguments) Example receiving `/gain` and replying to its sender; Output Channels `value`: ```ts // Target: chop import type { ChopHost } from '@avtools/native-webgpu/td-chop'; export async function setup(host: ChopHost) { const osc = await host.osc.open({ port: 9000 }); osc.onError((error) => console.warn('OSC:', error.message)); osc.onMessage((message, sender) => { const arg = message.args[0]; if (message.address !== '/gain' || !arg || (arg.type !== 'f' && arg.type !== 'i' && arg.type !== 'd')) return; if (!Number.isFinite(arg.value)) return; host.outputs.set('value', arg.value); osc.send({ address: '/received', args: [arg] }, sender).catch(console.warn); }); // Sending needs no inbound message; this sends to another known receiver. await osc.send({ address: '/ready', args: [true] }, { address: '127.0.0.1', port: 9001, }); } ``` Bundles deliver immediately in wire order, including future timetags. Each message reports its innermost bundle's raw 64-bit NTP timetag; a standalone message uses `1n`. Timetags do not schedule future callbacks. There is no automatic address-pattern matching: route addresses in your handler. Malformed packets, unsupported tags and nesting deeper than 16 are discarded as a whole and reported to `onError`. These APIs are available on TOP hosts too; update state for draw instead of using the CHOP-only outputs API. ## Build, activation and cleanup | Operator control | Behavior | | --- | --- | | TypeScript File | Selects one entry in a normal TS project | | Automatic Builds | Watches/compiles that entry and its dependency graph | | Build Script | Requests a build; does not override Automatic Reload | | Automatic Reload | Activates successful changed code and its declared controls; default on | | Reload | Adopts latest successfully available code, even if unchanged | | Reset | Restarts currently active code; does not adopt a pending newer build | First initialization loads available code even with Automatic Reload off. Identical rebuilds do not restart; enabling Automatic Reload adopts a pending change. Each operator controls activation independently, even with a shared entry. A failed build preserves the active running sketch. A runtime activation failure stops the old environment and does not roll back; edit/reload/reset to recover. A previously completed output may remain visible, which does not mean the old script is still running. Pending actions need a normal TD cook to take effect. Every activation creates a fresh isolate: module variables, globals, timers, promises, listeners and sockets start over. TOP resize and CHOP output-schema changes also restart the active source. A TOP recreates its device and renderer. There is no state-preserving hot module replacement or serialization of live JS state into the `.toe`. Source/config/assets must travel with the saved project. `host.onDispose(() => { ... })` registers short synchronous cleanup, called in reverse registration order while resources are still valid. Do not depend on an awaited cleanup, `finally`, or cancellation continuation completing during full reload. The host releases resources even if cleanup fails. Application-level task cancellation can be used normally while the generation remains alive. An uncaught callback exception/unhandled rejection stops the owning sketch and appears in diagnostics; `console.error` alone does not stop it. User code owns its error policy for promises it catches. A synchronous callback and microtask drain have a watchdog (1 second); async initialization has a 3-second wait limit. Keep callbacks much shorter for interactive work. Async I/O prevents ordinary read waits from occupying JS, but does not make JSON parsing or other CPU work async. Teardown joins workers and pending native file operations; slow filesystem/native driver calls can still delay it. These limits are not hard realtime guarantees. ### Project and build files Keep `tsconfig.json` at this project's root and extend `./sdk/tsconfig.json`. It supplies local aliases and the host type profile. The mixed template includes `td-top-runtime.d.ts`; replace that include with `td-runtime.d.ts` for a CHOP-only project. Additional tsconfig `paths` replaces inherited paths, so preserve required SDK aliases when customizing it. Avoid hardcoding paths into the avTools source repository: the generated SDK is local to this project. Local `.wgsl` imports yield strings. Recognized material/compute shader suffixes produce generated wrappers under `generated/`. Files under `.avtools/` are caches; do not select or edit them as your source. The native builder compiles each entry with its dependencies, so unrelated entry errors need not block it. Imports may point outside the project or through symlinks, but those dependencies must also be available when sharing. npm installation is separate; the builder neither installs packages nor supplies missing Node/browser runtime APIs. Source selection precedence is TypeScript File, legacy Project Directory, Sketch DAT, then Source File. For new work use TypeScript File. Legacy DAT/source JS uses ordinary top-level callback functions and has no native TypeScript metadata extraction. `host.timing` supports compatibility scripts; new TS code should import `@avtools/core-timing` directly. ## Logging, diagnostics and verification Create an **Info DAT** targeting the operator. On its **Diagnostics** page choose **Info DAT View → Diagnostics** for build/reload state or **Logs** for console messages. This view setting is shared by all Info DATs targeting that operator. Log columns are `sequence`, `time_ms`, `generation`, `level`, `message`. Timestamps are monotonic since logger creation, not timeline time. Log Level defaults to Info (`log` and `info`); choose Debug for debug messages. It filters future messages only. History retains 256 entries, up to 4096 UTF-8 bytes each. Large/deep values are previewed with limits; formatting does not run getters or custom inspection code. No browser-style `%s`/`%o` substitution is performed. `console.error` is logging, not throwing. There is no automatic Textport or terminal mirroring. **Clear Logs** clears history/counters, preserving script state and sequence numbering. **Refresh Logs (No Script)** updates TD's cached metadata while paused without running JS, consuming a worker result, or activating queued resets/reloads. It takes effect through a metadata-only source cook. Force-cooking only the Info DAT may not refresh the source's cached table. Use Passive on observers when you do not want them to pull ordinary source cooks. Logs survive script reload/reset, but not deleting the operator or closing the project. Useful Info DAT fields: `build_state`, `build_diagnostics`, `reload_state`, `source_identity`, `log_retained`, `log_evicted`, `log_dropped`, `log_truncated`. Use an **Info CHOP** for numeric runtime measurements: | Operator | Useful channels | | --- | --- | | TOP | `output_age_frames`, `skipped_frames`, `worker_busy`, `cook_ms`, `worker_ms`, `input_download_ms`, `input_upload_ms`, `draw_submit_ms`, `readback_wait_ms`, `upload_enqueue_ms`, `blocking_wait_ms` | | CHOP | `submitted_request`, `accepted_request`, `completed_request`, `source_request`, `published_sequence`, `consumed_sequence`, `input_age_ms`, `publication_age_ms`, `reused_cooks`, `repeated_percent_120`, `coalesced_inputs`, `cook_ms`, `script_ms`, `worker_ms`, `blocking_wait_ms` | For TOPs, `output_age_frames == 0` means output was submitted in the current TD absolute frame; positive values indicate older output, and `-1` means unavailable or an invalid age after a seek. Sample it over running frames to count same-frame versus delayed results. For CHOPs, publication identity/age tells you about retained output; timers may publish multiple times from one accepted input request. `repeated_percent_120` measures reuse, not an exact fixed number of latency frames. TD's `cpuCookTime` does not include all concurrent worker CPU. TOP `upload_enqueue_ms` measures the TD upload call, not separate GPU completion. Sum submission and collection costs for pre-trigger mode. Readbacks and copies remain costs even on unified-memory Macs. Return Info DAT View to Diagnostics after inspecting logs to avoid repeatedly copying full log tables. Before calling a sketch finished, check the following in TD: 1. Build state is Ready and runtime warnings/errors are clear. 2. The required input wiring and output channel/sample configuration are explicit. 3. Representative input/parameter changes produce the expected output, including missing-input fallbacks. Pulses affect state as intended relative to onCook/draw. 4. Saving code and pressing Reset give the intended fresh state. A build error preserves the previous working code. Setup resources (files/ports) reopen. 5. If timing/OSC matters, verify state updates while playback is paused, then resumes presentation on the next cook; inputs remain the last accepted snapshot. 6. Measure at the intended resolution/buffer size and instance count. Do not infer same-frame latency from low TD CPU cook time alone. For a coding agent without TD access, build/typecheck and inspect the examples, then clearly state which runtime behavior still needs TD verification. Optional `avtools-build check-file ENTRY.ts top|chop` checks types; `build-file` also bundles. The CLI is a maintainer tool and is not required or shipped beside the plugins. The generated README and SDK are embedded in each plugin at build time; updating a plugin does not overwrite an existing generated project's files. ## Native MIDI API MIDI device input/output is built into the macOS TOP and CHOP. No browser MIDI, Node, Deno, npm install, or separately installed MIDI library is needed. See `sketches/midi/picture.ts`, `sketches/midi/channels.ts` (Output Channels: `value note velocity`), and `sketches/midi/explicit.ts`. Declare a device selector as literal entrypoint metadata: ```ts export const parameters = { Controller: { type: 'midiInput', label: 'MIDI Controller', page: 'MIDI' }, } as const; ``` Inside setup, use `host.midi.bindInput('Controller')`. Type the host as `ChopHost` or `Setup` to restrict binding names to MIDI parameters. The dropdown defaults to **None**, displays names, and stores device IDs. It preserves unavailable selections without choosing another device. Choices refresh when the menu is built (cached up to one second). The returned logical handle retains listeners when the selection changes. Each operator has independent subscriptions, so several TOPs/CHOPs can use the same controller. Changing selection closes the old connection and discards its pending messages. MIDI selection updates use a separate worker control path; ordinary `host.params` still represents the latest accepted cook snapshot. ```ts const controller = host.midi.bindInput('Controller', { rateHz: 250, rawCC: true, }); const unsubscribe = controller.on('cc', ({ controller, value, timeMs }) => { // Read current state, update state, or start a TimeContext task here. }); controller.on('noteOn', ({ note, velocity }) => { /* ... */ }); controller.onStatus(() => { console.log(controller.port, controller.connected, controller.error); }); ``` All callbacks run on this script's worker, independently of TD cooking, and have normal TimeContext lifetime ownership. They do not interrupt executing JS. Drawing/output consumption occurs on later cooks. Exceptions use the normal script error path. Do not do expensive per-message work unnecessarily. ### MIDI methods and types `host.midi` provides: - `listInputs()` / `listOutputs()`: arrays of `{id, name, manufacturer}`; manufacturer is currently `null`. IDs are opaque strings, not list indexes or portable device names. Re-select on another computer when necessary. - `bindInput(parameterName, options?)`: managed selector binding; requires a declared `midiInput` parameter. Can be used for several differently named inputs. - `await openInput(deviceId, options?)`: explicit connection; rejects if opening fails. This has the same listener interface but no parameter binding. - `await openOutput(deviceId)`: explicit MIDI output. `send(Uint8Array | number[])`, `noteOn(channel, note, velocity=100)`, `noteOff(channel, note, velocity=0)`, `cc(channel, controller, value)`, `pitchBend(channel, bend)`, `polyPressure(channel, note, pressure)`, `channelPressure(channel, pressure)`, `programChange(channel, program)`, and `close()`. Sends are immediate; native scheduled output is not exposed. Coordinate messages yourself if several scripts send to the same destination. - `stats`: cumulative native-runtime counters `droppedMessages`, `batches`, `queuedBatches`, `inputs`, `outputs`. A full runtime restart resets them. An input handle has `port` (or null), `connected`, `closed`, `error`, `onMessage(callback)`, `on(type, callback)`, `onStatus(callback)`, `reconnect()`, and `close()`. Listener registration returns an unsubscribe function. `connected` means a native connection was opened; it is not a live cable-health guarantee. Missing selections remain disconnected with `error`; **None** has no error. `reconnect()` retries explicitly. Hardware unplug/replug is not automatically reconnected. Handles close automatically on reload/reset/deletion; pending MIDI is discarded, with no replay or state restoration. Other operators continue. Input event types and fields (all include `channel` and `timeMs`): | Type | Additional fields | | --- | --- | | `noteOn`, `noteOff` | `note`, `velocity` | | `cc` | `controller`, `value` | | `pitchBend` | `bend` | | `polyPressure` | `note`, `pressure` | | `channelPressure` | `pressure` | | `programChange` | `program` | Channels are 0–15; normal values are 0–127; pitch bend is -8192–8191. Note-on velocity zero becomes note-off. `timeMs` retains the backend's source timestamp in milliseconds: compare deltas within a connection; do not subtract it from `performance.now()` or TD timeline time, or assume the epoch survives reconnect. ### Delivery and limits `rateHz` is an integer 1–1000 (default 250: approximately 4 ms batching), and `rawCC` is boolean (default true). Idle inputs do not poll. Batching reduces worker wakeups; raw CC still invokes handlers for each message. With `rawCC:false`, CC is latest-value-per-controller within a batch and unchanged values may be suppressed. Use raw CC for relative encoders, RPN/NRPN and other stateful message sequences. Pitch bend, pressure and program changes retain their existing latest-value coalescing. Note transitions are individually queued. Delivery is bounded: 32 open input/output connections per instance, native queues of 4096 raw messages/notes/raw CC entries, and a worker queue of 128 batches / 1 MiB. Overload drops messages and increments counters; it can lose note-offs. There is no lossless guarantee during overload or reload. Output sends accept up to 64 KiB. The current input supports MIDI 1.0 channel-voice messages, not SysEx, clock, transport, song position or MIDI 2.0/UMP. OSC's MIDI argument type is unrelated to opening native MIDI devices.

/**
 * Triangulate an outline.
 *
 * @param vertices A flat array of vertice coordinates like [x0,y0, x1,y1, x2,y2, ...].
 * @param holes An array of hole indices if any (e.g. [5, 8] for a 12-vertice input would mean one hole with vertices 5–7 and another with 8–11).
 * @param dimensions The number of coordinates per vertice in the input array (2 by default).
 * @return A flat array with each group of three numbers indexing a triangle in the `vertices` array.
 * @example earcut([10,0, 0,50, 60,60, 70,10]); // returns [1,0,3, 3,2,1]
 * @example with a hole: earcut([0,0, 100,0, 100,100, 0,100,  20,20, 80,20, 80,80, 20,80], [4]); // [3,0,4, 5,4,0, 3,4,7, 5,0,1, 2,3,7, 6,5,1, 2,7,6, 6,1,2]
 * @example with 3d coords: earcut([10,0,1, 0,50,2, 60,60,3, 70,10,4], null, 3); // [1,0,3, 3,2,1]
 */
export default function earcut(vertices: ArrayLike<number>, holes?: ArrayLike<number>, dimensions?: number): number[];

/**
 * Transforms multi-dimensional array (e.g. GeoJSON Polygon) into the format expected by earcut.
 * @example Transforming GeoJSON data.
 *     const data = earcut.flatten(geojson.geometry.coordinates);
 *     const triangles = earcut(data.vertices, data.holes, data.dimensions);
 * @example Transforming simple triangle with hole:
 *     const data = earcut.flatten([[[0, 0], [100, 0], [0, 100]], [[10, 10], [0, 10], [10, 0]]]);
 *     const triangles = earcut(data.vertices, data.holes, data.dimensions);
 * @param data Arrays of rings, with the first being the outline and the rest holes. A ring is an array points, each point being an array of numbers.
 */
export function flatten(
    data: ArrayLike<ArrayLike<ArrayLike<number>>>,
): { vertices: number[]; holes: number[]; dimensions: number };

/**
 * Returns the relative difference between the total area of triangles and the area of the input polygon. 0 means the triangulation is fully correct.
 * Used to verify correctness of triangulation
 * @param vertices same as earcut
 * @param holes same as earcut
 * @param dimensions same as earcut
 * @param triangles see return value of earcut
 * @example
 *     const triangles = earcut(vertices, holes, dimensions);
 *     const deviation = earcut.deviation(vertices, holes, dimensions, triangles);
 */
export function deviation(
    vertices: ArrayLike<number>,
    holes: ArrayLike<number> | undefined,
    dimensions: number,
    triangles: ArrayLike<number>,
): number;

# Typescript Type Definitions for WebGPU

This package defines Typescript types (`.d.ts`) for the upcoming [WebGPU standard](https://github.com/gpuweb/gpuweb/wiki/Implementation-Status).

Use this package to augment the ambient [`"dom"`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/compiler-options.html#compiler-options) type definitions with the new definitions for WebGPU.

## API style docs

This repo also generates typedoc docs here: https://gpuweb.github.io/types

## What are declaration files?

See the [TypeScript handbook](http://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-files/introduction.html).


## Integration into `"dom"` type definitions.

WebGPU types have been integrated into the [`"dom"`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/compiler-options.html#compiler-options) starting with TypeScript 6. It appears that
v6.0.4 and above will include a full set of WebGPU types and thus should not need the supplemental types from this repo.

Unfortunately some versions of TypeScript include a `"dom"` library which only contained a partial set of WebGPU types, preventing WebGPU code from building cleanly. This is confirmed
the case in TypeScript v6.0.3 and lower and TypeScript v7.0.2 and lower. To build WebGPU with the affected versions install the [`@types/web`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@types/web)
to be package v0.0.352 or greater, and use it instead of the built-in `"dom"` library:

Install:
```
npm install @types/web
```

Usage in `tsconfig.json`:
```js
{
  // ...
  "compilerOptions": {
    // ...
    "lib": ["esnext"], // Do not include "dom"!
    "types": ["@types/web"],
  }
}
```

For TypeScript v5 and below, this library is still necessary to provide WebGPU types.



## How can I use them?

### Install

- npm: `npm install --save-dev @webgpu/types`
- yarn: `yarn add --dev @webgpu/types`
- pnpm: `pnpm add -D @webgpu/types`

If you are on TypeScript < 5.1, you will also need to install `@types/dom-webcodecs`
as a sibling dependency. The version you need depends on the TypeScript version;
see the [tests](tests/) for examples.

### Configure

Since this package is outside DefinitelyTyped, the dependency won't be picked up automatically.
There are several ways to add a additional TypeScript type definition dependencies to your TypeScript project:

#### TypeScript `tsc` and `tsc`-based bundlers

In `tsconfig.json`:

```js
{
  // ...
  "compilerOptions": {
    // ...
    "types": ["@webgpu/types"]
  }
}
```

Or you can use `typeRoots`:

```js
{
  // ...
  "compilerOptions": {
    // ...
    "typeRoots": ["./node_modules/@webgpu/types", "./node_modules/@types"]
  }
}
```

#### Inline in TypeScript

This may work better if your toolchain doesn't read `tsconfig.json`.

```ts
/// <reference types="@webgpu/types" />
```

#### Webpack

If you use Webpack and the options above aren't sufficient (this has not been verified),
you may need the following in `webpack.config.js`:

```js
"types": ["@webgpu/types"]
```

#### Others?

Please contribute a PR to add instructions for other setups or improve existing instructions. :)


## How to update these types

- Make sure the submodule is checked out: `git submodule update --init`
- Pull `gpuweb` changes: `pushd gpuweb && git checkout main && git pull && popd`
- Install dependencies: `npm ci`
- Generate `generated/index.d.ts`: `npm run generate`
- Open a diff between `generated/index.d.ts` and `dist/index.d.ts`.
    The generated file is tracked by Git so you can see what has changed.
    Update the latter according to changes from the former.
    Note the `generated/` and `dist/` files are not the same.
    See below for intentional differences.
- Format the result: `npm run format`

### Intentional differences between generator output and final result

Most or all of these should be fixed in the generator over time.

- `any` changed to `object` for WebIDL `object`.

The following differences are TODO: should be changed in the final result.

- Deprecated items should be removed.
- TODO items should be fixed (e.g. make new additions no longer optional).
- Addition of Compatibility Mode items like `textureBindingViewDimension`.

The following differences will remain.

- `onuncapturederror` strongly typed.
- `addEventListener('uncapturederror')` type support.
- `getContext` definitions.
- `GPUExtent3DStrict` and `GPUOrigin2DStrict`.

### Publish a new npm package version

(only for people who have npm publish access)

* One line cmd to copy-n-paste (for ssh git user, and you'd better know what you are doing, if it failed at certain steps, you might need to clean up git tags before trying again)
  - `git checkout main && git pull git@github.com:gpuweb/types.git main && git submodule update --init && npm version patch && git push git@github.com:gpuweb/types.git main --tags && npm publish`
* Separate steps (better for publishing for the first time)
  * Make sure you are in the upstream repo, not your forked one. And make sure you are synced to latest commit intended for publish
    - `git checkout main`
    - `git pull https://github.com/gpuweb/types.git main`
      - (If you are using HTTPS regularly. You can use remote names like `origin`, just make sure you are referring to the right repo)
    - `git submodule update --init`
  * Create the version tag and commit, and push
    - `npm version patch`
    - `git push https://github.com/gpuweb/types.git main --tags`
  * publish the package
    - `npm publish --otp=<code>`
      - Replace `<code>` with the one-time password from your authenticator, since two-factors authentication is required to publish.
      - If you are doing for the first time, you will do `npm adduser` first and it will guide you through adding the npm account.

## Earcut

The fastest and smallest JavaScript polygon triangulation library. 3KB gzipped.

[![Node](https://github.com/mapbox/earcut/actions/workflows/node.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mapbox/earcut/actions/workflows/node.yml)
[![Average time to resolve an issue](http://isitmaintained.com/badge/resolution/mapbox/earcut.svg)](http://isitmaintained.com/project/mapbox/earcut "Average time to resolve an issue")
[![Percentage of issues still open](http://isitmaintained.com/badge/open/mapbox/earcut.svg)](http://isitmaintained.com/project/mapbox/earcut "Percentage of issues still open")
[![](https://img.shields.io/badge/simply-awesome-brightgreen.svg)](https://github.com/mourner/projects)

#### The algorithm

The library implements a modified ear slicing algorithm,
optimized by [z-order curve](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-order_curve) hashing
and extended to handle holes, twisted polygons, degeneracies and self-intersections
in a way that doesn't _guarantee_ correctness of triangulation,
but attempts to always produce acceptable results for practical data.

It's based on ideas from
[FIST: Fast Industrial-Strength Triangulation of Polygons](http://www.cosy.sbg.ac.at/~held/projects/triang/triang.html) by Martin Held
and [Triangulation by Ear Clipping](http://www.geometrictools.com/Documentation/TriangulationByEarClipping.pdf) by David Eberly.

#### Why another triangulation library?

The aim of this project is to create a JS triangulation library
that is **fast enough for real-time triangulation in the browser**,
sacrificing triangulation quality for raw speed and simplicity,
while being robust enough to handle most practical datasets without crashing or producing garbage.
Some benchmarks using Node 0.12:

(ops/sec)         | pts  | earcut    | libtess  | poly2tri | pnltri    | polyk
------------------| ---- | --------- | -------- | -------- | --------- | ------
OSM building      | 15   | _795,935_ | _50,640_ | _61,501_ | _122,966_ | _175,570_
dude shape        | 94   | _35,658_  | _10,339_ | _8,784_  | _11,172_  | _13,557_
holed dude shape  | 104  | _28,319_  | _8,883_  | _7,494_  | _2,130_   | n/a
complex OSM water | 2523 | _543_     | _77.54_  | failure  | failure   | n/a
huge OSM water    | 5667 | _95_      | _29.30_  | failure  | failure   | n/a

The original use case it was created for is [Mapbox GL](https://www.mapbox.com/mapbox-gl), WebGL-based interactive maps.

If you want to get correct triangulation even on very bad data with lots of self-intersections
and earcut is not precise enough, take a look at [libtess.js](https://github.com/brendankenny/libtess.js).

#### Usage

```js
const triangles = earcut([10,0, 0,50, 60,60, 70,10]); // returns [1,0,3, 3,2,1]
```

Signature: `earcut(vertices[, holes, dimensions = 2])`.

* `vertices` is a flat array of vertex coordinates like `[x0,y0, x1,y1, x2,y2, ...]`.
* `holes` is an array of hole _indices_ if any
  (e.g. `[5, 8]` for a 12-vertex input would mean one hole with vertices 5–7 and another with 8–11).
* `dimensions` is the number of coordinates per vertex in the input array (`2` by default). Only two are used for triangulation (`x` and `y`), and the rest are ignored.

Each group of three vertex indices in the resulting array forms a triangle.

```js
// triangulating a polygon with a hole
earcut([0,0, 100,0, 100,100, 0,100,  20,20, 80,20, 80,80, 20,80], [4]);
// [3,0,4, 5,4,0, 3,4,7, 5,0,1, 2,3,7, 6,5,1, 2,7,6, 6,1,2]

// triangulating a polygon with 3d coords
earcut([10,0,1, 0,50,2, 60,60,3, 70,10,4], null, 3);
// [1,0,3, 3,2,1]
```

If you pass a single vertex as a hole, Earcut treats it as a Steiner point.

Note that Earcut is a **2D** triangulation algorithm, and handles 3D data as if it was projected onto the XY plane (with Z component ignored).

If your input is a multi-dimensional array (e.g. [GeoJSON Polygon](http://geojson.org/geojson-spec.html#polygon)),
you can convert it to the format expected by Earcut with `earcut.flatten`:

```js
const data = earcut.flatten(geojson.geometry.coordinates);
const triangles = earcut(data.vertices, data.holes, data.dimensions);
```

After getting a triangulation, you can verify its correctness with `earcut.deviation`:

```js
const deviation = earcut.deviation(vertices, holes, dimensions, triangles);
```

Returns the relative difference between the total area of triangles and the area of the input polygon.
`0` means the triangulation is fully correct.

#### Install

Install with NPM: `npm install earcut`, then import as a module:

```js
import earcut from 'earcut';
```

Or use as a module directly in the browser with [jsDelivr](https://www.jsdelivr.com/esm):

```html
<script type="module">
    import earcut from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/earcut/+esm';
</script>
```

Alternatively, there's a UMD browser bundle with an `earcut` global variable (exposing the main function as `earcut.default`):

```html
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/earcut/dist/earcut.min.js"></script>
```

- [mapbox/earcut.hpp](https://github.com/mapbox/earcut.hpp) (C++11)
- [JaffaKetchup/dart_earcut](https://github.com/JaffaKetchup/dart_earcut) (Dart)

seedrandom.js
=============
[![Build Status](https://travis-ci.org/davidbau/seedrandom.svg?branch=master)](https://travis-ci.org/davidbau/seedrandom)
[![NPM version](https://badge.fury.io/js/seedrandom.svg)](http://badge.fury.io/js/seedrandom)
[![Bower version](https://badge.fury.io/bo/seedrandom.svg)](http://badge.fury.io/bo/seedrandom)

Seeded random number generator for JavaScript.

Version 3.0.5

Author: David Bau

Date: 2019-09-14

Can be used as a plain script, a Node.js module or an AMD module.


Script tag usage
----------------

```html
<script src="//cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/seedrandom/3.0.5/seedrandom.min.js">
</script>
```

```js
// Make a predictable pseudorandom number generator.
var myrng = new Math.seedrandom('hello.');
console.log(myrng());                // Always 0.9282578795792454
console.log(myrng());                // Always 0.3752569768646784

// Use "quick" to get only 32 bits of randomness in a float.
console.log(myrng.quick());          // Always 0.7316977467853576

// Use "int32" to get a 32 bit (signed) integer
console.log(myrng.int32());          // Always 1966374204

// Calling seedrandom with no arguments creates an ARC4-based PRNG
// that is autoseeded using the current time, dom state, and other
// accumulated local entropy.
var prng = new Math.seedrandom();
console.log(prng());                // Reasonably unpredictable.

// Seeds using the given explicit seed mixed with accumulated entropy.
prng = new Math.seedrandom('added entropy.', { entropy: true });
console.log(prng());                // As unpredictable as added entropy.

// Warning: if you call Math.seedrandom without `new`, it replaces
// Math.random with the predictable new Math.seedrandom(...), as follows:
Math.seedrandom('hello.');
console.log(Math.random());          // Always 0.9282578795792454
console.log(Math.random());          // Always 0.3752569768646784

```

**Note**: calling `Math.seedrandom('constant')` without `new` will make
`Math.random()` predictable globally, which is intended to be useful for
derandomizing code for testing, but should not be done in a production library.
If you need a local seeded PRNG, use `myrng = new Math.seedrandom('seed')`
instead.  For example, [cryptico](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cryptico),
an RSA encryption package, [uses the wrong form](
https://github.com/wwwtyro/cryptico/blob/9291ece6/api.js#L264),
and thus secretly makes `Math.random()` perfectly predictable.
The cryptico library (and any other library that does this)
should not be trusted in a security-sensitive application.


Other Fast PRNG Algorithms
--------------------------

The package includes some other fast PRNGs.  To use Johannes Baagøe's
extremely fast Alea PRNG:


```html
<script src="//cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/seedrandom/3.0.5/lib/alea.min.js">
</script>
```

```js
// Use alea for Johannes Baagøe's clever and fast floating-point RNG.
var arng = new alea('hello.');

// By default provides 32 bits of randomness in a float.
console.log(arng());               // Always 0.4783254903741181

// Use "double" to get 56 bits of randomness.
console.log(arng.double());        // Always 0.8297006866124559

// Use "int32" to get a 32 bit (signed) integer.
console.log(arng.int32());         // Always 1076136327
```

Besides alea, there are several other faster PRNGs available.
Note that none of these fast PRNGs provide autoseeding: you
need to provide your own seed (or use the default autoseeded
seedrandom to make a seed).

|PRNG name  | Time vs native | Period      | Author               |
|-----------|----------------|-------------|----------------------|
|`alea`     |  1.95 ns, 0.9x | ~2^116      | Baagøe               |
|`xor128`   |  2.04 ns, 0.9x | 2^128-1     | Marsaglia            |
|`tychei`   |  2.32 ns, 1.1x | ~2^127      | Neves/Araujo (ChaCha)|
|`xorwow`   |  2.40 ns, 1.1x | 2^192-2^32  | Marsaglia            |
|`xor4096`  |  2.40 ns, 1.1x | 2^4096-2^32 | Brent (xorgens)      |
|`xorshift7`|  2.64 ns, 1.3x | 2^256-1     | Panneton/L'ecuyer    |
|`quick`    |  3.80 ns, 1.8x | ~2^1600     | Bau (ARC4)           |

(Timings were done on node v0.12.2 on a single-core Google Compute Engine
instance.  `quick` is just the 32-bit version of the RC4-based PRNG
originally packaged with seedrandom.)


CJS / Node.js usage
-------------------

```
npm install seedrandom
```

```js
// Local PRNG: does not affect Math.random.
var seedrandom = require('seedrandom');
var rng = seedrandom('hello.');
console.log(rng());                  // Always 0.9282578795792454

// Global PRNG: set Math.random.
seedrandom('hello.', { global: true });
console.log(Math.random());          // Always 0.9282578795792454

// Autoseeded ARC4-based PRNG.
rng = seedrandom();
console.log(rng());                  // Reasonably unpredictable.

// Mixing accumulated entropy.
rng = seedrandom('added entropy.', { entropy: true });
console.log(rng());                  // As unpredictable as added entropy.

// Using alternate algorithms, as listed above.
var rng2 = seedrandom.xor4096('hello.')
console.log(rng2());
```

Starting in version 3, when using via require('seedrandom'), the global
`Math.seedrandom` is no longer available.


Require.js usage
----------------

Similar to Node.js usage:

```
bower install seedrandom
```

```
require(['seedrandom'], function(seedrandom) {
  var rng = seedrandom('hello.');
  console.log(rng());                  // Always 0.9282578795792454
});
```


Network seeding
---------------

```html
<script src=//cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/seedrandom/3.0.5/seedrandom.min.js>
</script>
<!-- Seeds using urandom bits from a server. -->
<script src=//jsonlib.appspot.com/urandom?callback=Math.seedrandom>
</script>

<!-- Seeds mixing in random.org bits -->
<script>
(function(x, u, s){
  try {
    // Make a synchronous request to random.org.
    x.open('GET', u, false);
    x.send();
    s = unescape(x.response.trim().replace(/^|\s/g, '%'));
  } finally {
    // Seed with the response, or autoseed on failure.
    Math.seedrandom(s, !!s);
  }
})(new XMLHttpRequest, 'https://www.random.org/integers/' +
  '?num=256&min=0&max=255&col=1&base=16&format=plain&rnd=new');
</script>
```

Reseeding using user input
--------------------------

```js
var seed = Math.seedrandom();        // Use prng with an automatic seed.
document.write(Math.random());       // Pretty much unpredictable x.

var rng = new Math.seedrandom(seed); // A new prng with the same seed.
document.write(rng());               // Repeat the 'unpredictable' x.

function reseed(event, count) {      // Define a custom entropy collector.
  var t = [];
  function w(e) {
    t.push([e.pageX, e.pageY, +new Date]);
    if (t.length < count) { return; }
    document.removeEventListener(event, w);
    Math.seedrandom(t, { entropy: true });
  }
  document.addEventListener(event, w);
}
reseed('mousemove', 100);            // Reseed after 100 mouse moves.
```

The "pass" option can be used to get both the prng and the seed.
The following returns both an autoseeded prng and the seed as an object,
without mutating Math.random:

```js
var obj = Math.seedrandom(null, { pass: function(prng, seed) {
  return { random: prng, seed: seed };
}});
```


Saving and Restoring PRNG state
-------------------------------

```js
var seedrandom = Math.seedrandom;
var saveable = seedrandom("secret-seed", {state: true});
for (var j = 0; j < 1e5; ++j) saveable();
var saved = saveable.state();
var replica = seedrandom("", {state: saved});
assert(replica() == saveable());
```

In normal use the prng is opaque and its internal state cannot be accessed.
However, if the "state" option is specified, the prng gets a state() method
that returns a plain object the can be used to reconstruct a prng later in
the same state (by passing that saved object back as the state option).


Version notes
-------------

The random number sequence is the same as version 1.0 for string seeds.

* Version 2.0 changed the sequence for non-string seeds.
* Version 2.1 speeds seeding and uses window.crypto to autoseed if present.
* Version 2.2 alters non-crypto autoseeding to sweep up entropy from plugins.
* Version 2.3 adds support for "new", module loading, and a null seed arg.
* Version 2.3.1 adds a build environment, module packaging, and tests.
* Version 2.3.4 fixes bugs on IE8, and switches to MIT license.
* Version 2.3.6 adds a readable options object argument.
* Version 2.3.10 adds support for node.js crypto (contributed by ctd1500).
* Version 2.3.11 adds an option to load and save internal state.
* Version 2.4.0 adds implementations of several other fast PRNGs.
* Version 2.4.2 adds an implementation of Baagoe's very fast Alea PRNG.
* Version 2.4.3 ignores nodejs crypto when under browserify.
* Version 2.4.4 avoids strict mode problem with global this reference.
* Version 3.0.1 removes Math.seedrandom for require('seedrandom') users.
* Version 3.0.3 updates package.json for CDN entrypoints.
* Version 3.0.5 removes eval to avoid triggering content-security policy.

The standard ARC4 key scheduler cycles short keys, which means that
seedrandom('ab') is equivalent to seedrandom('abab') and 'ababab'.
Therefore it is a good idea to add a terminator to avoid trivial
equivalences on short string seeds, e.g., Math.seedrandom(str + '\0').
Starting with version 2.0, a terminator is added automatically for
non-string seeds, so seeding with the number 111 is the same as seeding
with '111\0'.

When seedrandom() is called with zero args or a null seed, it uses a
seed drawn from the browser crypto object if present.  If there is no
crypto support, seedrandom() uses the current time, the native rng,
and a walk of several DOM objects to collect a few bits of entropy.

Each time the one- or two-argument forms of seedrandom are called,
entropy from the passed seed is accumulated in a pool to help generate
future seeds for the zero- and two-argument forms of seedrandom.

On speed - This javascript implementation of Math.random() is several
times slower than the built-in Math.random() because it is not native
code, but that is typically fast enough.  Some details (timings on
Chrome 25 on a 2010 vintage macbook):

* seeded Math.random()          - avg less than 0.0002 milliseconds per call
* seedrandom('explicit.')       - avg less than 0.2 milliseconds per call
* seedrandom('explicit.', true) - avg less than 0.2 milliseconds per call
* seedrandom() with crypto      - avg less than 0.2 milliseconds per call

Autoseeding without crypto is somewhat slow, about 20-30 milliseconds on
a 2012 windows 7 1.5ghz i5 laptop, as seen on Firefox 19, IE 10, and Opera.
Seeded rng calls themselves are fast across these browsers, with slowest
numbers on Opera at about 0.0005 ms per seeded Math.random().

/**
